title: Chapter 13: Quid Pro Quo
content: The pin will not go in.

Wren has the apron up on the chain fall, the hinge blocked with a wedge of oak, and the new pin in her fist. It came off a lathe at the machine shop on Mill Street on Tuesday for sixty dollars and two free crossings. It is four thousandths too wide, and she knows that the way she knows most things now, by trying it eleven times.

The flashlight is in her teeth. The old pin sheared on the twelfth of September when she put the apron down hard on the east ramp. It is out in the gravel under three inches of silt and she has not gone looking.
The water is loud tonight. October came in on Tuesday, and the river has the flat metal sound it gets when the air goes cold, and the yard smells of tar and wet rope.
Headlights come down Ferry Lane at 9:40 and stop at the gate. She does not turn around. There are four people in this county who would drive down that lane at night, and three of them would honk.
A truck door. City shoes on gravel. The particular apologetic crunch of a man who does not want to be heard arriving.
"You are doing that in the dark," Theo says.
She takes the flashlight out of her mouth.
"It is the only time I have."

He stands at the edge of the light with a folder under his arm and no jacket. A white shirt with the sleeves rolled, a tie he has taken off and put in his pocket. He looks at the apron, the chain fall, the pin.
"That is not going to fit."
"It will fit."
"It is four thousandths over."
She looks at him.
"I can see it from here," he says, which is a lie, and they both let it stand, because the alternative is to talk about why he is here.

He puts his hand out for the flashlight. She gives it to him, and he holds it steady at the height she needs without being told, and that is the worst thing he has done all week, because it means he remembers how she works.
The pin goes in to the shoulder and stops. She taps it with the heel of her hand. It rings, once, like something very far away being struck.
"You cut the housing," she says.
"What?"
"In September. Somebody cut the cable housing in the night and I have been assuming it was the Authority, because the Authority is the only thing in this town with a reason."
"I was in Columbus." He says it flatly, without heat. "I have been in Columbus since the fourth of September. There are forty people who can tell you where I was on the eighth."
"Then who."

"Somebody who did not want you crossing." He moves the light along the cable where it comes up the bank, and the new housing sits on it like a bandage. "That is not the same as somebody who wanted your grandfather dead. This town has men in it who would cut a cable to stop a wedding and go to church on Sunday."
She works the pin another half inch. It is not going.
"Say why you came," she says.
He sets the folder on the toolbox, opens it, and takes out one sheet, and holds it where the light falls on it. It is a Form 9. She knows the shape of it the way she knows her own handwriting.
"I can have this paid in nine days," he says.

She reads it. Name of decedent: Elias Aubrey. Date of loss: 12 September 2026. Relationship of claimant: granddaughter. And section 6, cause, as certified, typed and not handwritten, in a machine's even letters.
Act of river.
"Nine days," she says.
"Nine days from the day you sign. The payment order goes out of Columbus, not the district. It does not go through Hollis. It does not go through the drawer."
"And the hearing."

"There is no hearing if there is no dispute. I withdraw the filings, the county vacates the docket, and the condemnation goes forward on its own calendar. That part I cannot stop. That part was set in August."
"Four minutes," she says.
"Four minutes. And then the ferry goes and you have ninety thousand dollars and a roof that does not leak and you stop being the woman in the paper."
She turns the sheet over. There is nothing on the back.
"And the forty-one."
"They stay pending."
"Say it whole."

He looks at the water. "The forty-one stay pending. They were always going to stay pending. You moved them from a drawer in a basement to a docket in Columbus and they are still pending, and the only thing your filings changed is that a clerk has to write a number on a receipt."
"That is not the only thing they changed."
"No," he says. "It is not."

She sets the pin down on the toolbox and picks up the form with both hands, the way she picks up the log, and reads it again, all three pages of it, because there are three pages, and the second page is the one he did not mention.

Page two, section 11. Consideration for release. Ninety thousand dollars, payable on execution. Below that, three lines, and the third line is this: claimant shall deliver to the Authority the vessel's log, all volumes, for archival purposes.
"You brought me the same paper she did," she says. "On a nicer night."
"It is not the same paper."
"It has the same clause in it. Clause eleven. Schedule B. You did not even change the number."
"The number is the number." His jaw works. "The archive is climate controlled. It is a room with a door and a lock and a hygrometer. Your kitchen has a wood stove in it."
"My kitchen has me in it."
"That is what I am afraid of."
She puts the form down and puts her hand flat on it, and the paper is warm from the light.
"Whose idea was nine days," she says.
"Mine."
"Whose idea was the form."
He is quiet. The river goes past the piling with the long tearing sound it makes when the level is dropping.
"Mine," he says.

She has known him in three seasons and she has never once heard him lie about a fact. He lies by leaving things out, and he has left out the thing she is going to ask, and she can feel the shape of the hole in the sentence.
"Theo."
"Say it."
"You wrote the survey."
"I wrote the survey."

"Page four recommends a ninety second rise. You told the board a slower rise would not clear the silt." She keeps her voice level, because level is the only tool she has that he cannot take. "And page four has a date on it. The twelfth of September."
"That is a target date."
"It was a Thursday."

"It was a Thursday in the window. The window closes at the end of September. You run it in the window, or you run it in April with the intake half blocked and the town on bottles." He says it fast, the way he says things he has said before, in rooms with better chairs. "The date on page four is not a decision. It is an estimate."
"Then who decided."
"Columbus."
"Who decided," she says again, "that it would be the twelfth, at night, with no siren."
"The siren is not my office."
"That is not what I asked."
He looks at her. In the light from the flashlight, held down now at his leg, his face is all shadow and one cheekbone, and she can see him decide something, and she can see him decide it twice.
"I am going to lose the seal," he says.
"You said that on the phone."

"I did not say it on the phone. I said I could not stamp it. That is different." He puts the light on the ground, pointing up, and the yard goes strange and tall. "If this goes to a hearing, the survey is an exhibit. The board reads page four. The board reads the recommendation and the date and the ninety seconds, and they ask me whether I understood what ninety seconds does to a river at Mile 9 with no warning, and I say yes, and then I am a man who used to be an engineer."
"You would still have the job."
"I would have a desk."

"Your grandfather," she says, and stops, because it is not her grandfather, it is hers. "My grandfather had a boat and a cable and a book. Fifty-one years. He did not have a seal. He had a hand that people could read."
"This is not a comparison."
"No. It is a question about what you would be if they took the one thing away, and you have just told me." She picks the pin up again. "You would be a man with a desk."
"Take the money," he says. "Not for me. Nine days is real. Nine days is a furnace and a roof and a winter where you do not count fares in a coffee can."
"I have counted fares in a coffee can my whole life. It is not the worst thing that has happened to me this year."
"That is a low bar."
"It is the only bar I have got."
She takes the form and folds it in three and puts it inside her jacket, in the pocket where her grandfather kept his license, and Theo watches her do it and his face changes.
"That is my copy."
"It is a signed document from a certifying officer of the Basin Authority that says act of river." She buttons the pocket. "I am going to file it as an exhibit."
"It is not a filing. It is an offer. It is confidential."
"Then you should not have brought it to my house."
"Wren."

"It says what the Authority thinks the cause is. It says it in type. It has a date on it and a signature on it and it is the first piece of paper in twenty-five days that admits the Authority considered the question." She hears her own voice and it is not loud. "You have given me the exhibit, Theo. You drove two hours to hand me the exhibit."
He stands there with the flashlight on the ground between them, throwing his shadow up the side of the shed.
"I could take it back," he says.
"You could."
He does not. She knew he would not, and the knowing is not a comfort.

He picks up the light and puts it on the toolbox, and closes his folder, and stands with his hand on the truck door for a moment, and the cold has got into his shirt and he is not pretending otherwise anymore.
"Nine days," he says. "The offer stands until the docket moves."
She walks him to the truck, because the yard is dark and she is not going to stand in it.
At the gate he stops with his hand on the post, and she asks it.
"Theo. On the twenty-second of August, when you signed page four, did you know the gate was set to run on the twelfth?"

"I did not ask what Columbus decided," she says. "I did not ask what the board knew or what she knew or what the schedule said. I asked what you knew, on the twenty-second of August, in your own hand, on page four."
The river goes past. Somewhere down the bank a heron lifts off with that sound they make, like a hinge.
He gets in and puts both hands on the wheel and does not start it.
Then he starts it.
She stands at the gate and watches the taillights go up the lane and turn toward Columbus, and waits until the red is gone and the dark is ordinary.
He did not say no.
She walks back to the apron and picks up the pin and turns it around in her fingers, and it is tapered, and she has had it backwards for forty minutes.
It goes in the first time. Two taps and it seats, and the apron swings free on the hinge, and the sound it makes is the sound it made in August.
highlight: A tapered hinge pin finally seats, and Theo comes to the ferry house with a quiet fix she refuses.
